result:
The repair shop had one rule: you had to tell the truth about how the thing broke.

This was written on a small card beside the till. Most customers assumed it was a joke until the owner slid their belongings back across the counter.

“Try again,” she would say.

A man brought in a watch and said he’d dropped it.

“Try again.”

He looked at the stopped hands. “I threw it at a wall.”

She opened a drawer for a new spring.

A woman brought in a radio that had belonged to her father.

“It just stopped working.”

The owner waited.

“I took it apart because I thought there might be something inside.”

“What sort of something?”

“I don’t know. A note.”

The owner nodded and reached for her smallest screwdriver.

People began to misunderstand the rule. They arrived prepared to confess infidelities, petty thefts, opinions they had kept to themselves for forty years. The owner interrupted them.

“I need to know what happened to the toaster.”

One afternoon a boy brought in a blue ceramic bowl, wrapped in a school jumper. There were five large pieces and a little heap of crumbs.

“I broke it,” he said.

“How?”

“With a hammer.”

“All right.”

“You’re not going to ask why?”

“Does why affect the glue?”

He considered this. “Probably not.”

She laid the pieces out on the counter. He watched her turn one of them twice before finding where it belonged.

“Can you make it so nobody can tell?”

“No.”

He began gathering up the pieces, but she put a hand beside the broken rim.

“I can make it hold water again.”

The boy left the bowl with her.

When he came back on Friday, she filled it at the little sink behind the counter. Water darkened the blue glaze. A crooked pale seam ran from the rim to the base.

He carried it to the window and stood there a while, looking underneath for a drip.

“How much?”

“Three pounds.”

He paid in coins, then dried the bowl carefully with his sleeve.
